transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2025-10-28 09:00 PDT / 16:00Z
- Duration: 63 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Chen, Diego Alvarez, Priya Singh, Oliver Grant, Chen Wei

Summary (auto):
Brief triage of an accuracy regression observed after customer applied an INT8 GPTQ-style conversion on a 7B model in their on-prem environment. Discussion focused on mixed-precision fallbacks, KV-cache compatibility when switching precisions at runtime, batching effects on latency SLO, and on-prem packaging constraints (container permissions, KMS, kernel drivers).

Topics:
- Root cause hypotheses for accuracy drift after quantization
- Mixed-precision scheduling vs model variant routing
- KV-cache invalidation and warmup strategies for precision switches
- On‑prem runtime constraints (CUDA driver versions, mmap, numa)
- Plan for instrumentation, dataset for repro, and remediation options

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: okay, hi everyone, thanks for joining on short notice. we wanted to do a focused triage on the INT8 conversion issues you reported, Priya, is that right?
[00:12] Priya: yep. thanks, Maya. we've got a regression — about a 6 to 8 point hit on Rouge-L and a weird failure mode on some longer context prompts. it only shows up when we run the gptq-quantized build in our on‑prem cluster.
[00:26] Diego: can you remind us of the conversion stack? like which toolchain — gptq, awq, anything custom? and are you mixing FP16 kernels anywhere?
[00:36] Priya: we used a community GPTQ fork from internal ops, then applied an AWQ-like per-channel scale patch — it's kinda hybrid. we still run some attention kernels in FP16 because we patched in a fallback for softmax stability in layer norm.
[00:49] Chen: also want to add that our on‑prem infra is locked at CUDA 11.7 and we have A10x GPUs with slightly older drivers, so we can't move to the latest runtime easily.
[01:02] Diego: that helps. older drivers do change kernel scheduling and sometimes expose numeric corner cases. question: do you preserve KV cache across precision switch during streaming? like are you switching model variants mid‑session?
[01:17] Oliver: ah, yes — we tried a cheap trick to keep latency low: start in FP16 tiny-model variant, then switch into INT8 quantized variant for longer outputs because of cost constraints. we preserved kv cache blobs and reused them.
[01:30] Maya: that's a red flag — KV cache is not generally bit-compatible across quantization granularities because activation distributions change and scale factors differ. reusing raw cache can produce numerical drift and break attention alignment.
[01:44] Priya: hmm. That is exactly where the failures show up — longer context prompts get incoherent after the switch point.
[01:50] Diego: two immediate hypotheses: one, per-layer activation outliers cause AWQ/GPTQ to pick bad clamping ranges and that cascades with cached k/v mismatches; two, runtime differences (CUDA kernels) produce slightly different rounding which, when compounded, cause divergence for long-context sequences.
[02:07] Priya: are there known mitigation patterns? ops wants something automatable — we can't do a manual flush for every switch.
[02:15] Diego: options — prefer 1) keep model variant and precision consistent across a session (no KV reuse), 2) if you must reuse KV across precisions, do an on-the-fly re-quantize of the cache with the new scale factors — that's expensive, or 3) use a thin checkpointing: drop last N tokens' cache and warm up with a short prefix to re-align.
[02:33] Oliver: re-quantize the cache sounds heavy. dropping tokens might be more acceptable but we need to know warmup cost.
[02:40] Diego: typically warmup of 20–40 tokens will resync attention for most models, but it depends on the layerwise sensitivity — some models show path dependence deeper in the stack.
[02:51] Chen: what about mixed-precision scheduling? can we let runtime choose FP16 for certain layers at inference time? we were hoping for an automated scheduler so we can keep latency SLO but avoid accuracy hits.
[03:02] Diego: yes — Redwood runtime supports layerwise mixed-precision; we can mark the top (earlier) layers to use FP16 and only quantize bottom layers to INT8. but the quantization scheme must be aware of per-layer ranges. we also need to ensure chosen kernels are available in your driver stack.
[03:20] Priya: kernel availability — is there a solid compatibility matrix you can share? we have strict change control.
[03:26] Maya: yep — we'll send our runtime kernel compatibility matrix and the minimal CUDA/driver versions. there are also small patches we can apply to the container (set CAP_SYS_ADMIN?) for memory mapping; we'll include those notes in the security packet.
[03:38] Priya: great. the SOC2 folks will want that.
[03:41] Oliver: one more thing — we noticed latency regressions when enabling dynamic batching after quantization. batch latencies increased by 10–15% under tail loads. any idea why?
[03:51] Diego: two likely causes: 1) quantized kernels sometimes run slower on particular sequence-length mixes due to less fused ops and memory reshuffles, and 2) batch scheduling interacts poorly with KV-cache reuse; cache copy and re-quantization overhead can add to scheduling jitter.
[04:08] Priya: is there a way to profile which layers are causing the slowdown?
[04:11] Diego: yes — we can run a per-layer timing trace with perf markers. we'll use the Redwood onprem profiler (lightweight) to collect kernel time, memcpy, and quant/dequant time. it requires adding a small env var and a profiling agent.
[04:24] Maya: action: Diego will provide the profiler script; Priya will run it on a representative workload. Diego, can you also annotate the trace with activation statistics?
[04:33] Diego: yep. I'll export per-layer activation min/max/mean/std, and frequency of outliers. that'll help decide if we need per-channel clipping/enumeration or stochastic rounding.
[04:43] Chen: stochastic rounding — do we have production experience with it for regression issues? we tried it once and results were mixed.
[04:49] Diego: it's a tradeoff. stochastic rounding reduces systematic bias but can add variance; for sensitive tasks with long contexts it sometimes helps. AWQ's strategies and some GPTQ variants use different rounding heuristics — some customers prefer AWQ for fewer outliers but AWQ can be larger in memory.
[05:03] Priya: memory — our limit is ~22GB per GPU. the quantized artifact is smaller but AWQ builds were slightly bigger due to per-channel tables. any suggestions?
[05:12] Diego: you can try hybrid quant: INT8 for weights, FP16 for activations in hot layers, and per-block quant for large linear layers. also Redwood has a mode for compressed per-channel tables that trades a tiny perf hit for memory savings.
[05:29] Priya: interesting. what about validation? we have a long eval suite, but running full benchmarks on on‑prem every time is costly. can Redwood provide a quick smoke diff that catches these regression classes?
[05:41] Maya: yes, we often run a focused regression sentinel — ~200 prompts representing your fast‑fail cases and a small holdout. Diego can set up an eval harness that runs locally against your cluster and reports statistical significance for metric deltas.
[05:53] Diego: we'll implement paired bootstrap on the prompt suite and surface a per-prompt delta table — that helps find the failure modes quickly.
[05:59] Oliver: timeline — we need a plan that minimally affects our SLOs. if we revert to FP16 for a while to stabilize, can we do a canary route for a subset of users?
[06:08] Maya: absolutely. Redwood routing supports canary based on model tags and percentage traffic. you can route, say, 10% to FP16 and 90% to quantized, and monitor rollback triggers on perplexity/latency thresholds.
[06:20] Priya: are the metrics we should watch per-token latency, 99th latency, and a QA accuracy metric?
[06:26] Diego: yes — and add alignment checks for long-context drift (we'll provide a small alignment score that compares attention-based token overlap for prefixes).
[06:34] Chen: curious — you mentioned re-quantizing KV cache earlier. is that something Redwood runtime could do automatically?
[06:39] Diego: in principle yes — a background job could scan cache entries and convert scales. but it's expensive and we haven't shipped it as a default because of memory copying costs. for on‑prem we could prototype a streaming re-quantizer that operates async and throttles to not exceed tail SLOs.
[06:55] Priya: that could be an ideal compromise if it doesn't break tail latency.
[06:58] Diego: right, we would throttle and expose a policy: immediate flush, async re-quantize, or drop last N tokens.
[07:06] Maya: ok, to recap next steps: Diego will provide profiler script and activation exporter; Priya will run the profiler and upload artifacts; Maya will send the kernel/driver compatibility matrix and security docs. we'll then run the eval harness and propose a mixed-precision config to test canary.
[07:21] Priya: that works. one last quick question — any known gotchas with on‑prem KMS when using Redwood private? we need to prove keys never leave HSM.
[07:30] Maya: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM integrations. we'll share our integration notes; on-prem we can do a local HSM connector so keys are never exported. I'll include that in the docs.
[07:40] Chen: perfect. thanks.
[07:42] Oliver: thanks all.
[07:44] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule the bench session next week.

Closing notes (auto):
- Primary suspected root cause: KV-cache reuse across precision variants combined with layerwise activation outliers and older CUDA kernel differences.
- Short-term mitigations: avoid mid-session precision switches, drop N-token cache window when switching, run canary routing to FP16 fallback.
- Long-term: instrument per-layer activation distributions, consider hybrid mixed-precision policy, prototype async KV re-quantizer.
